newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.AFRICA GOLD MINES MAY HAVE SOLD FORWARD - ANALYSTS.
newsitem.headline: S.AFRICA GOLD MINES MAY HAVE SOLD FORWARD - ANALYSTS.

text.p: Fairly large quantities of gold may have been sold forward recently due to an attractive rand gold price which South African producers would be eager to lock in, analysts told Reuters on Friday.
Bullion crumbled in London earlier and dealers attributed it to heavy selling by speculators. But some suggested that South African gold producers were pressuring the market.
Due to the rand losing more than 30 percent of its value on the dollar since February, South African gold mines have gleefully reaped the benefits of record high rand gold prices.
On October 30, the price of bullion in rands nudged above 1,800 rand per ounce. It remains comfortably above 1,780 rand.

"There could well be selling coming from South African producers at this sort of price. The reason being that in rand terms the gold price has risen rather spectacularly over the past year," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.
"If we can hedge in rand terms off this base then we can lock in a very attractive contango," he added.

A contango occurs when selling forward wins a better price than selling at the spot price. The contango in forward gold sales is based on the difference between the cost of leasing gold from a bank and current interest rates.

Analysts said overseas interest rates were satisfactory at the moment and that South African gold producers would be foolish not to grab the current attractive gold price, lock it in and cash in on it at a later date.

"Overseas interest rates give the contango but you have to take a view on the rand. Our rand contango looks fairly attractive. The lending rates aren't bad at the moment. They've come right down from January this year," an analyst said.

"One cannot expect realistically that the gold price even in rand terms can rise at this rate on a continuous basis," another analyst said adding that the rand might possibly steady early next year or at least weaken at a slower rate.
Analysts said that while it was unlikely any producer would let a good hedge slip through its fingers if possible, no South African gold mine would "dump" bullion onto the market.
It is the policy of South African gold mines -- such as Anglo American Corp of South Africa Ltd -- to gradually supply more gold onto the market, they said.

"I would take the Anglo view of regular selling over a longer-term programme. There have probably been some fairly big forwards coming through in this sort of market but they won't go and dump the crown jewels. Their policy is to continually to add to the market and now is a good time," an analyst said.
Analysts said that pressure might also be coming form Australian producers whose gold price -- in Australian dollar terms -- has fallen on the back of their currency strengthening.
"There is a little bit of panic selling from Australia because their gold price has dropped about 20 percent over the year because of the strength of their currency, an analyst said.
"So while they're largely hedged producers you might find them now doing some hedging to just to make sure that their gold price is a bit higher a year from now."
Another analyst denied the gold price was pressured.

"I'm not of the opinion that the gold price is under any pressure at the moment. If one looks at what has happened over the last week or so, there has been a dramatic improvement in volatilities and that volatility usually preceds a run in the gold price."
